params.question: Which of the following is NOT a legitimate reason to order an investigation in a surgical patient?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Confirming or excluding a diagnosis is one of the four legitimate reasons. The governing question remains: will this result change what I do?

answers.text: To screen for incidental findings in an asymptomatic patient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The four legitimate reasons are: confirm or exclude a diagnosis, define disease extent, establish a baseline before treatment, and assess fitness for surgery. Ordering tests 'just to check' without a clinical question leads to over-investigation and cascade harms — one incidental finding triggering more tests, biopsies, and sometimes unnecessary operations.
Defining disease extent (staging) is a legitimate reason. The key discipline is ensuring every test answers a specific clinical question that will change management.

answers.text: To assess the patient's fitness for surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Assessing fitness for surgery is one of the four legitimate reasons. The real test is always: will this result change what I do?

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four legitimate reasons: confirm or exclude a diagnosis, define disease extent, establish a baseline, and assess fitness. 'Screening for incidental findings' is not one of them.
Well done. Every investigation must serve a specific purpose. Testing without a clinical question is over-investigation, not thoroughness.

params.question: A 50-year-old asymptomatic man requests a CA 19-9 test during a routine health check to screen for pancreatic cancer. What is the most appropriate response?

answers.text: Order the test as it can detect pancreatic cancer early

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CA 19-9 is not a reliable screening test. It can be raised in benign conditions such as biliary obstruction. In a low-prevalence asymptomatic population, a positive result carries a very low positive predictive value.

answers.text: Order the test along with CT abdomen for completeness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adding imaging to an inappropriate screening test compounds the harm — this is the cascade effect, where one incidental finding leads to further tests, biopsies, and sometimes unnecessary operations.

answers.text: Decline the test because tumour markers are not reliable screening tools in asymptomatic individuals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tumour markers like CA 19-9 are designed for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence in patients with a known cancer. They are not validated for screening asymptomatic individuals — exactly the error illustrated in the opening case.

answers.text: Order the test but only if CEA and AFP are also included in the panel

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adding more tumour markers does not improve screening accuracy. CEA and AFP, like CA 19-9, have roles in monitoring known cancers, not in screening well patients.

overallFeedback.feedback: Tumour markers (CEA, CA 19-9, AFP, PSA, beta-hCG, CA-125) are designed for monitoring treatment response and recurrence, not for screening asymptomatic patients. A normal level does not exclude cancer; a raised level can arise from benign causes.
Exactly. Tumour markers monitor known cancers — they do not screen for new ones. Recall the opening case: ordering CA 19-9 to screen a well patient caused real harm.

interactions.label: Screening and early diagnosis are the same strategy — both detect cancer in pati

params.question: Screening and early diagnosis are the same strategy — both detect cancer in patients who already have symptoms, but screening uses simpler tests.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: That statement is false. Screening and early diagnosis are distinct strategies. Screening targets people with no symptoms, using population-level tests to find disease before it declares itself. Early diagnosis means recognising and investigating symptoms promptly once they appear. Both exploit the same biological window but in different groups.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — that statement is false. Screening targets asymptomatic individuals, aiming to find disease in the pre-clinical detectable phase before any warning signs appear. Early diagnosis, by contrast, means acting promptly when symptoms are already present. They target different populations and use different tools.

params.question: A new marker detects a rare cancer five years before symptoms appear. Patients diagnosed by the marker appear to survive seven years from diagnosis, compared with three years from symptom onset without the marker. Which phenomenon must be excluded before concluding the marker improves outcomes?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Overdiagnosis means detecting indolent lesions that would never cause harm. Here the cancer has a definite three-year symptomatic course, so it is not indolent. The key concern is whether the apparent survival gain is real or an artefact of earlier detection.

Correct. Lead-time bias makes survival appear longer simply because diagnosis was earlier, without changing the actual date of death. The five-year lead time explains the apparent four-year gain (7 − 3 = 4 ≈ 5). A valid screening programme must demonstrate reduced population mortality, not merely longer survival from diagnosis.

Selection bias (e.g. healthier volunteers in screening trials) can confound results, but the scenario specifically describes the artefact of measuring survival from an earlier diagnosis date — the hallmark of lead-time bias.

Stage migration (Will Rogers phenomenon) occurs when reclassification moves patients between stage groups. The scenario describes apparent survival improvement from earlier detection, which is the definition of lead-time bias.

overallFeedback.feedback: Lead-time bias inflates apparent survival by shifting the diagnosis date earlier without changing the date of death. A five-year lead time makes three-year survival look like seven. Reduced mortality — not longer survival — is the valid measure of screening benefit.
Well done. Lead-time bias is why a sound screening programme must be justified by reduced population mortality, not by longer apparent survival from diagnosis.
